video_title: Scaling Laws: Algorithmic Disgorgement with Christina Lee
gist: Legal scholar Christina Lee traces 'algorithmic disgorgement' -- the FTC-pioneered remedy forcing companies to delete an entire trained AI model -- from its 2019 Cambridge Analytica origins through its spread to state AGs and international regulators like South Korea's PIPC, arguing the remedy increasingly strains against modern AI's complex, multi-actor data supply chains.

insights.claim: Algorithmic disgorgement is an FTC-pioneered legal remedy that forces a company to delete an entire trained AI model -- not merely stop using it or delete the underlying training data -- when the model's creation or use is found illegal.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest (GW Law visiting professor)
insights.so_what: AI companies exposed to data-provenance or deceptive-collection claims face a remedy far harsher than a fine or injunction -- the entire model asset can be zeroed out, not just a dataset.
insights.quote: just say get rid of the whole model

insights.claim: The remedy originated in the FTC's 2019 Cambridge Analytica settlement: because Cambridge Analytica's Facebook app deceptively collected personally identifiable information after claiming it wouldn't, the FTC required deletion of any models trained on that data, reasoning that deleting the source data alone would leave the trained model (the actual thing of value) intact.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Establishes the legal precedent baseline: any company that used deceptively-collected data to train a model, even if the raw data is later deleted, can still be forced to destroy the resulting model.

insights.claim: Since the 2019 Cambridge Analytica case, the FTC ordered algorithmic disgorgement in roughly a dozen settlements, making it a fairly regular enforcement tool for about the first ten such settlements before slowing under the current FTC leadership.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Gives investors a rough base rate (~12 cases over ~6 years) for how often U.S. federal regulators have actually deployed the harshest AI remedy, useful for calibrating enforcement-probability models.

insights.claim: Most FTC tech enforcement happens through negotiated settlement rather than litigation, which gives the agency room to craft creative remedies like algorithmic disgorgement, but those remedies must stay within bounds of reasonableness or the company could choose to litigate instead; Cambridge Analytica was a procedural outlier, resolved by summary judgment (not settlement) because the company was already defunct by the time the order came through.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Explains why disgorgement demands are typically negotiated and bounded in practice rather than maximally punitive -- relevant to modeling worst-case outcomes for a company under FTC investigation.

insights.claim: The Texas Attorney General sought algorithmic disgorgement in a 2022 lawsuit against Meta over its facial-recognition models, building on fact patterns from earlier Meta face-recognition litigation; the case settled out of court and, as far as the guest knows, did not actually result in disgorgement, but the request itself shows state AGs adopting the FTC's remedy playbook.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: State attorneys general are an expanding, less predictable source of algorithmic-disgorgement risk for AI/biometric companies beyond federal FTC action.

insights.claim: In 2025, South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) ordered algorithmic disgorgement against Alipay over cross-border data transfer issues, marking an international regulator's adoption of the remedy outside the U.S.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Companies operating AI/data models across borders -- particularly Asian fintech and payments platforms -- face algorithmic-disgorgement exposure abroad, not only from U.S. regulators.

insights.claim: The guest cites the EU AI Act's ongoing implementation delay, alongside a recent change in FTC leadership, as evidence that global AI-regulation momentum -- including disgorgement-style remedies -- is currently stalled in a period of uncertainty rather than steadily escalating.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Near-term AI regulatory-compliance risk pricing may be overstated given the simultaneous stall in both U.S. and EU rule-making momentum -- worth revisiting if either resumes.

insights.claim: Christina Lee's paper frames algorithmic disgorgement as splitting into two types: 'database' disgorgement, where the model's creation/training process was tainted by illegal conduct (e.g., Cambridge Analytica's deceptive data collection), versus 'use-based' disgorgement, where the model itself was deployed illegally or improperly regardless of how cleanly it was trained.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Investors assessing an AI company's legal exposure should separate these two risk categories, since the underlying facts, defenses, and remediation paths differ substantially between them.

insights.claim: The FTC's 2023 Rite Aid settlement marked a shift toward use-based disgorgement logic: Rite Aid was ordered to delete its in-store facial-recognition models because the models were deployed improperly (falsely flagging customers for shoplifting due to horrendous accuracy), not primarily because the underlying training data was illegally collected.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Even companies with clean data provenance face disgorgement risk if a deployed AI model causes discriminatory or harmful real-world outcomes -- broadening exposure beyond data-sourcing compliance alone.

insights.claim: The EU AI Act includes product-recall-style remedies for AI systems that violate its mandates, which the guest sees as a plausible future vector for formal 'use-based' algorithmic disgorgement in Europe, though the Act's ongoing delay makes the timeline uncertain.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Watch EU AI Act implementation for a formal recall-style remedy that could become an international template for use-based disgorgement enforcement.

themes.theme: Modern AI's Complexity Strains the Remedy

insights.claim: Lee argues algorithmic disgorgement made sense for Cambridge-Analytica-style cases involving a single, clearly culpable actor, but is increasingly ill-suited to modern AI because the 'algorithmic supply chain' now spans many actors sourcing data from disparate places, making it much harder to cleanly attribute tainted data to one party's illegal conduct.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: As foundation models rely on broad, multi-sourced datasets, blanket disgorgement becomes legally harder for regulators to justify cleanly against any single company -- reduces tail risk of full-model-deletion outcomes for large, diversified-data-source labs, but increases litigation complexity and unpredictability.

insights.claim: Lee frames the appropriateness of disgorgement for general-purpose AI models as a cost-benefit test: regulators should weigh the harm of continued use of a tainted or misused model against the disruption of pulling a widely-relied-upon general-purpose model out of circulation, favoring narrower, more tailored remedies when a blanket ban would do more harm than good.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Frontier/general-purpose model providers may have a stronger practical defense against full disgorgement than narrow single-purpose model providers (e.g., a discriminatory resume-screening model), since deleting a narrow tool causes less disruption -- relevant to differential regulatory-risk assessment across AI business models.

insights.claim: The host raises a hypothetical in which a major AI lab violates FTC Act Section 5 the way Rite Aid or Cambridge Analytica did, noting that algorithmic disgorgement of a frontier AI model would have major ramifications for the stock market and for the trajectory of U.S. AI capability; the guest declines to predict whether or when such a watershed enforcement action will occur.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A frontier-lab disgorgement order is a low-probability, high-impact tail-risk scenario with potential market-wide relevance (not just an isolated compliance cost) -- worth monitoring as enforcement posture shifts.

insights.claim: Machine unlearning -- post-processing a trained model to remove the influence of specific tainted data points as if they were never used, without deleting the whole model -- is proposed as a more surgical alternative to full algorithmic disgorgement, but the guest states the technology is not yet practicably available.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: A technology to watch: if machine unlearning becomes technically viable, it could materially cut the tail risk of full-model disgorgement for AI companies with partial data-taint issues, making remediation far cheaper than total model loss.

insights.claim: Lee suggests machine unlearning would be most useful when only a small fraction of a model's training data is problematic, letting the model retain most of its functionality while the tainted subset is removed -- but she notes full-taint cases like Cambridge Analytica, where the entire dataset was deceptively collected, would remain unsuited to this approach.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Not a universal fix -- investors evaluating a target company's exposure should scrutinize what fraction of its training data is legally at risk, since unlearning only helps at the margin.

insights.claim: Lee notes the FTC has 'dialed back' on ordering algorithmic disgorgement following a recent change in agency leadership, but cautions this doesn't mean the remedy is dead, given its continuing adoption by state AGs (Texas) and international regulators (South Korea's PIPC).
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Reduced federal FTC enforcement activity should not be read as reduced overall regulatory risk -- state and international regulators are picking up the enforcement mantle on algorithmic disgorgement.

insights.claim: When pressed for a prediction on whether a 'watershed moment' (a major lab hit with algorithmic disgorgement) will force a broader reckoning on the remedy's appropriateness, Lee declines, stating flatly that predictions in this field tend to be wrong -- reflecting genuine uncertainty among AI-policy specialists about the field's near-term direction.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Even domain experts see AI-regulation trajectory as highly unpredictable in the near term -- investors should avoid over-indexing on any single confident regulatory forecast for AI enforcement.
insights.quote: one thing I've learned in this business is don't make predictions because it's going to be wrong

insights.claim: Lee's current research extends her disgorgement work into how traditional agency law applies -- and fails to apply -- to agentic AI, mapping which actors in an agentic AI ecosystem bear legal accountability when multiple AI agents interact.
insights.speaker: Christina Lee, guest
insights.so_what: Companies building agentic AI products should watch for forthcoming legal scholarship that could shape liability frameworks -- i.e., who is responsible when an autonomous AI agent's actions cause harm -- relevant to product and liability risk modeling.
